newsitem.title: USA: Republicans say Clinton budget alive, not yet kicking.
newsitem.headline: Republicans say Clinton budget alive, not yet kicking.

text.p: Congressional Republicans pronounced President Clinton's new budget "alive" Thursday but said that his opening bid would not erase the deficit by 2002 as promised.
"As for the whole budget: Well, I suppose that you could say it's alive, but definitely not kicking," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said.

Clinton sent Congress a $1.69 trillion budget proposal that cut $98.4 billion in taxes over five years, slashed $100 billion from Medicare health care for the elderly and reached a $17 billion surplus in 2002.
Republican budget leaders said if the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office economic assumptions were applied, the budget would post a $50 billion deficit in 2002.

"It does not balance in the year 2000," House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich said. The Ohio Republican unfurled a map of the United States and said the budget differences were as if Republicans started a race to California from New York, while Clinton started in Chicago.

Despite the complaints about what needed fixing in Clinton's budget, Republicans were careful to say it was a good starting point for discussion. Clinton is expected to meet with Congressional leaders Tuesday.
On what in the past has been a key contentious issue between the White House and Congress, Kasich said: "The president has moved in our direction on Medicare."
"This is a very good starting point," Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici said. "I do not think this budget is dead on arrival," the Republican from New Mexico added.
The tone was more conciliatory than in past years when Republicans have trashed the president's budget as it landed on the Capitol's steps.

In the last Congress budget negotiations fell apart and forced two government shutdowns that the public blamed on Republicans. Learning from that experience, Republicans have promised to work in a bipartisan manner.
The White House said if its budget and economic forecasts were wrong, it was prepared to rescind $22 billion in proposed tax cuts, and cut spending in order to reach balance by 2002.
The president's proposed tax provisions aimed to benefit families, encourage higher education, expand retirement savings and ease taxes on home sales.

Clinton proposed a $500 per child tax credit for low- and middle-income families, saving taxpayers $46 billion through 2002. He also proposed a $1,500 tax credit or a $10,000 tax deduction for college tuition and training.
Republicans said Clinton's tax proposals would only help a specific group of Americans, not the general public.

"I am hopeful that we can work with this Administration to hammer out a real budget, and perhaps we can salvage some of the President's ideas,"Assistant House majority leader, Tom DeLay of Texas said.

"I am more optimistic about our prospects for achieving success in our consideration of a balanced budget proposal now than I have been for a long time," added Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota.

Daschle said he based his optimism partly on the credibility of the budget proposal, the attitude of Republicans on working to achieve a meaningful budget proposal and the "desire of both sides to try get this done in a much more constructive way than we did in the 104th Congress."
The White House said it was pleased Clinton's budget proposal was being treated seriously by Republicans.

"We certainly expect criticism. We certainly expect alternative ideas to come forward," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry. "But the most encouraging thing to the president is that this budget is being received seriously and it clearly will be the basis of further discussions on the Hill. It is not being cast aside as a document dead on arrival."
